ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A small block $P$ with mass $m=5\text{kg}$ is placed on a horizontal ground. Under the action of a horizontal pushing force of magnitude $F = 25\text{N}$, it moves in a straight line at a constant speed. The gravitational acceleration $g$ is taken as $10\text{m/s}^2$, and the maximum static friction force is equal to the sliding friction force.

1. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction between $P$ and the horizontal surface.
2. If the thrust $F$ is changed to be directed downward at an angle of $37^\circ$ to the horizontal, while the magnitude of the thrust $F$ remains unchanged, $\sin37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos37^\circ = 0.8$, find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on $P$.

Vertically, the normal force is N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. Thus the coefficient of kinetic friction is μ_k = f_k / N = 25 / 50 = 0.5. Angled downward push: Resolve the same 25 N force into components. method.method_draft: Use direct force balance in two separate free-body diagrams. First, for the initial horizontal push, read that the block moves at constant speed, so net horizontal force is zero; therefore kinetic friction equals the applied force, f_k = 25 N. Read m = 5 kg and g = 10 m/s^2, so the normal force is N = mg = 50 N, giving μ_k = f_k/N = 25/50 = 0.5. Second, when the same force is angled downward by 37°, resolve it into components: horizontal component F cos37° = 25 × 0.8 = 20 N and downward vertical component F sin37° = 25 × 0.6 = 15 N. The friction needed to balance the horizontal tendency is 20 N. Check the available maximum friction using the increased normal force N' = mg + F sin37° = 65 N, so f_max = μN' = 0.5 × 65 = 32.5 N. Since 20 N < 32.5 N, friction adjusts to 20 N.

method.method_draft: Use a work/energy interpretation for the first part and a threshold test for the second. In the initial case the block moves at constant speed, so over any displacement the net work is zero. The horizontal push does positive work Fd and kinetic friction does negative work f_kd, hence f_k = F = 25 N. With the horizontal push there is no vertical component, so N = mg = 50 N and μ_k = 25/50 = 0.5. In the angled case, the downward force component increases the normal reaction to 50 + 25(0.6) = 65 N, so the maximum possible friction is 0.5 × 65 = 32.5 N. The applied force does positive work Fd, and kinetic friction does negative work f_k d. Thus Fd - f_k d = 0, so f_k = F = 25 N. Since the push is horizontal, the normal force is N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. Therefore the coefficient of kinetic friction is μ_k = f_k / N = 25 / 50 = 0.5.

Second part: The same force F = 25 N is now directed downward at 37° to the horizontal.
